title: Web Development
tagline: Web applications that are still fast a year after launch.
summary: Marketing sites, dashboards, internal tools and storefronts, built to be maintained rather than rebuilt.
problem: Most web projects are judged on how they look the week they ship. The bill arrives later: the page that was quick with fifty rows crawls at fifty thousand, nobody can add a field without touching six files, and the one person who understood the deploy has moved on. None of that is visible at launch, which is exactly why it keeps happening.
outcomes: A codebase your next developer can read without a handover call
Performance budgets that are enforced in CI, not hoped for
Accessibility built in from the first component rather than retrofitted
A deploy that can be reversed in one step

whatWeDo.title: Application development
whatWeDo.description: Dashboards, admin panels, internal tools and customer-facing applications in React and TypeScript, with server-side rendering where it earns its cost and static rendering where it does not.

whatWeDo.title: Marketing and content sites
whatWeDo.description: Statically generated sites wired to a headless CMS, so a marketing team can publish without a deploy and the site still scores well on Core Web Vitals.

whatWeDo.title: Commerce
whatWeDo.description: Storefronts and checkout flows on headless commerce platforms, with the payment and inventory paths covered by tests because those are the ones that cost money when they break.

whatWeDo.title: API and data layer
whatWeDo.description: REST and typed RPC layers, database schema design, indexing and query work. Most "the app is slow" tickets end here rather than in the interface.

whatWeDo.title: Accessibility and performance
whatWeDo.description: WCAG 2.2 AA as a build requirement, keyboard paths tested by hand, and a performance budget that fails the build when it is exceeded.

whatWeDo.title: Migration and replatforming
whatWeDo.description: Moving an existing site off a framework or host that no longer fits, in reviewable stages, without a big-bang cutover weekend.

whatYouGet: The full source, in your repository, under your account, from the first commit
A README that a developer who has never met us can follow to a running local environment
Architecture notes explaining why things are where they are
A deployment pipeline with preview environments and one-step rollback
Tests covering the paths where a failure costs you money
whatsNotIncluded: Brand identity, logo design or naming
Copywriting and content strategy, though we will tell you where the content is doing the heavy lifting
Paid marketing, SEO campaigns or link building
timeline: Typically six to twelve weeks, scoped after a discovery call

process.title: Discovery
process.description: We work out what the software has to do, who uses it, and what already exists. If a smaller version of this would answer the question faster, we say so here rather than after the invoice.

process.title: Technical plan
process.description: Architecture, data model, third-party dependencies and the risks we can see, written down. You approve a scope and a shape before anyone writes code.

process.title: Build in reviewable slices
process.description: Working software every week on a preview URL, in pull requests small enough to actually read. You see progress rather than hearing about it.

process.title: Harden
process.description: Accessibility pass, performance budget, error tracking, backups and the rollback path. This is part of the build, not a phase you can cut when the date slips.

process.title: Handover
process.description: Documentation, a walkthrough with whoever takes it on, and access transferred to your accounts. You are not locked to us afterwards.

seo.title: Web Development
seo.description: Web applications, dashboards and content sites in React and TypeScript, built to be maintained. Accessibility and performance budgets enforced in CI.

title: Product Engineering
tagline: From first version to something a team can run.
summary: SaaS and platform work: the multi-tenancy, billing, permissions and operational plumbing that a product needs once real customers arrive.
problem: The first version of a product is the easy half. What breaks a young SaaS is everything the demo never needed: a second customer whose data must not touch the first one's, a failed payment that silently keeps an account active, a background job that retries forever, and a support request nobody can answer because there is no admin view. These are not features anyone asks for, and they decide whether the product survives its first hundred users.
outcomes: Tenant isolation you can explain to a security reviewer
Billing that stays in step with access, including on failure and refund
Background work that fails loudly and can be replayed
An admin surface so support does not mean a database query

whatWeDo.title: MVP to first customers
whatWeDo.description: The smallest version that answers the real question, built so the second version is not a rewrite. We are explicit about which shortcuts are deliberate and what they will cost to undo.

whatWeDo.title: Multi-tenancy and permissions
whatWeDo.description: Tenant isolation at the data layer rather than in application conditionals, plus roles and permissions that survive the first enterprise customer asking for custom access.

whatWeDo.title: Billing and subscriptions
whatWeDo.description: Subscription lifecycle wired to a payment provider: trials, upgrades, downgrades, dunning, proration and cancellation, with webhooks that are idempotent because they will be delivered twice.

whatWeDo.title: Background jobs and integrations
whatWeDo.description: Queues, scheduled work and third-party integrations with retry limits, dead-letter handling and alerting. A job that fails silently is worse than one that never ran.

whatWeDo.title: Observability
whatWeDo.description: Structured logging, error tracking, uptime and the handful of product metrics worth watching, wired to reach a person instead of a dashboard nobody opens.

whatWeDo.title: Scaling work
whatWeDo.description: Finding and fixing the specific query, index or N+1 that is actually slow, rather than adding infrastructure and hoping.

whatYouGet: A product that a team other than ours can operate and extend
Runbooks for the failures that are likely rather than the ones that are interesting
An admin interface for the support questions you will actually get
Monitoring and alerting configured and tested, not just installed
A written architecture decision record for the choices that are expensive to reverse
whatsNotIncluded: Market research, pricing strategy or go-to-market work
24/7 on-call, unless it is agreed separately as part of a retainer
timeline: Three to six months for a first release, then ongoing

process.title: Shape the problem
process.description: What the product must do, for whom, and what has to be true for it to be worth building. We push back here if the scope is larger than the question.

process.title: Architecture and decisions
process.description: Data model, tenancy strategy, auth approach and the integrations. The decisions that are expensive to reverse get written down with their reasoning.

process.title: Build the spine first
process.description: Auth, tenancy, billing and deployment before features, because retrofitting any of them into a working product costs several times more than starting with them.

process.title: Feature iterations
process.description: Weekly increments on a preview environment, prioritised together and re-planned as you learn from real usage.

process.title: Operate
process.description: Monitoring, runbooks and either a handover to your team or an ongoing retainer with us. Both are fine; we tell you which we think fits.

seo.title: Product Engineering
seo.description: SaaS and platform engineering: multi-tenancy, billing, permissions, background jobs and observability. From first release to a product a team can run.

title: Mobile Development
tagline: Apps that work on the train, not just on the demo Wi-Fi.
summary: Cross-platform iOS and Android applications in React Native, with the offline behaviour, release process and store work that mobile actually requires.
problem: Mobile punishes assumptions that the web forgives. The connection drops mid-write. The user is two versions behind and will not update. A rejected release costs a week, and a bug you shipped is live until Apple approves the fix. Teams that treat a mobile app as a web app in a smaller window discover all of this after launch, from their reviews.
outcomes: A defined offline story rather than a spinner and a hope
Old app versions that keep working against a changing API
A repeatable release process instead of one person's laptop
Crash reporting that maps to real source, not minified frames

whatWeDo.title: Cross-platform applications
whatWeDo.description: One React Native codebase for iOS and Android, dropping to native modules where a platform capability genuinely requires it rather than as a default.

whatWeDo.title: Offline and sync
whatWeDo.description: Local persistence, an explicit conflict-resolution rule and a queue for writes made without a connection. Decided at design time, because it cannot be added later without touching everything.

whatWeDo.title: API versioning for mobile
whatWeDo.description: Backend contracts that keep working for the users who will not update, and a deprecation path that does not brick installed apps.

whatWeDo.title: Push and deep links
whatWeDo.description: Notification handling across both platforms including permission states, plus deep links that survive a cold start.

whatWeDo.title: Release engineering
whatWeDo.description: Automated builds, TestFlight and Play internal testing tracks, staged rollout, and over-the-air updates for the changes that qualify for them.

whatWeDo.title: Store submission
whatWeDo.description: Store listings, privacy declarations, and the review-rejection cycle. We have read the guidelines so you do not have to.

whatYouGet: An app in your own App Store and Play Console accounts, never ours
Signing credentials and certificates handed over in an encrypted manager
A documented release process any developer on your team can run
Crash reporting with readable stack traces
The store listing assets and privacy declarations the platforms require
whatsNotIncluded: Fully native Swift or Kotlin rewrites of an existing app
App store optimisation and paid user acquisition
timeline: Two to four months to first store release

process.title: Platform decisions
process.description: Which platforms, which minimum OS versions, what has to work offline, and which native capabilities are genuinely required. These four answers determine most of the cost.

process.title: Foundation
process.description: Navigation, state, local persistence and the API contract. The offline rule is decided now, because it is not something that can be retrofitted.

process.title: Build with real devices
process.description: Weekly TestFlight and Play internal builds on actual hardware. Simulators hide performance problems and every permission dialog.

process.title: Release preparation
process.description: Store listings, privacy declarations, screenshots and the review submission, with time budgeted for the rejection that may well come.

process.title: Post-launch
process.description: Crash monitoring, staged rollout and a first patch release, because there is always a first patch release.

seo.description: Cross-platform iOS and Android apps in React Native, with offline handling, API versioning, release engineering and store submission.

title: Codebase Rescue
tagline: Take over the codebase nobody wants to touch.
summary: Audit, stabilisation and ongoing maintenance for software that was built fast — by a previous agency, a departed developer, or an AI coding tool — and now has to be safe to run.
problem: Working software and safe software are different things, and the gap only becomes visible at the worst moment. We open codebases and find live API keys in the git history, permission checks written in the browser, backups that have never once been restored, and errors caught and thrown away so nothing ever alerts. The people who built these are not careless. They shipped under pressure with tools that do not warn you which parts are missing — and AI coding assistants, which now write a large share of this code, warn you least of all.
outcomes: A written, severity-rated picture of what is actually wrong
Secrets rotated and removed from history, not just from the current files
Backups you have watched being restored
Alerts that reach a person before a customer does

whatWeDo.title: Audit
whatWeDo.description: Three to five days reading everything: the code, the full git history where deleted secrets still live, the schema and its indexes, the dependency tree, and the deployment path. It ends in a written report with every finding rated by severity and by what it would cost you, plus a walkthrough call.

whatWeDo.title: Stabilisation
whatWeDo.description: Closing what the audit found. Credentials rotated and purged from history, authorisation moved server-side, automated backups configured and restored in front of you, monitoring wired to alert a human, vulnerable dependencies upgraded in reviewable steps, and a rollback path put in place.

whatWeDo.title: Ongoing maintenance
whatWeDo.description: Security patching on a schedule, backup restore tests that actually run, uptime and error monitoring answered by us rather than by you, and a written monthly report. This is what stops a stabilised system drifting back.

whatWeDo.title: Documentation and handover
whatWeDo.description: Most rescued codebases have no documentation at all. We write the architecture notes, the runbooks and the deployment procedure as we go, so the knowledge is not trapped in whoever last touched it.

whatWeDo.title: Taking over from a departed team
whatWeDo.description: Where the original developer or agency is gone, we reconstruct how the system works from the code itself, then take responsibility for it.

whatWeDo.title: Continuing the roadmap
whatWeDo.description: Once a codebase is stable and we know it properly, we build on it. We do not add features to a system we have not read.

whatYouGet: A written report with a plain-language summary at the front for non-technical readers
Every finding rated critical, high, medium or low, with the actual consequence spelled out
A prioritised fix list ordered by risk rather than by effort
Working, verified backups and a rollback procedure you have seen used
Monitoring and alerting that reaches a person
whatsNotIncluded: Penetration testing or formal security certification — we find the obvious holes, we are not an accredited auditor
A guarantee that an audit finds every defect. Nobody can honestly offer that.
Rewrites sold as patches. If a rewrite is the right answer we say so, including when it costs us the work.
New features before the codebase is stable
timeline: Audit in three to five days; stabilisation usually one to three weeks

process.title: Mutual NDA
process.description: Signed before you grant any access at all. It covers your code, your data and anything else we happen to see.

process.title: Read-only access
process.description: An audit needs to read your code, not change it. No write access, no deploy access, no production database.

process.title: The audit
process.description: Three to five days of reading. If we find something genuinely urgent — a live credential in a public repository — you hear that the same hour, not in the report.

process.title: Report and walkthrough
process.description: The written report, then an hour on a call going through it. What you do next is entirely your decision, and taking the report to your own developer is a perfectly good outcome.

process.title: Stabilise, then maintain
process.description: If you want the work done, it arrives as small reviewable pull requests on a working branch. Your main branch is untouched until you approve a merge.

seo.title: Codebase Rescue
seo.description: Audit, stabilisation and maintenance for software built fast — by a previous agency, a departed developer or an AI coding tool. Read-only access, NDA first.
